questions_asked: When a neighbor calls in a giant-hornet sighting, what is the first thing your field team wants from that person?
Among callers who don't have a photo, which kind of person is most likely to actually have caught or killed the wasp, or can send a body to the lab?
How many reports does a state department like Washington's realistically have staff to investigate in a month during an active hornet scare?
Besides a clear photo, what single piece of a sighting story makes you trust it most, and what makes you doubt it?
How quickly, in days, should your team move on a new report near a known active hornet area before it stops being worth chasing?
When would officials say for sure the hornet is gone from a state, and how long do they keep looking before calling it eradicated?
When a fresh giant-hornet sighting shows up in a town far from any known nest, do you rush to check it or handle it like the others?
When big news coverage of a hornet nest breaks, how much does the call-in volume spike, and which kind of calls surge most?
After winter, when you first spot giant hornets again in spring, do you treat that as the outbreak starting over or as the same infestation?
During peak hornet season, do you check new reports every day or in batches, and how often do you refresh your suspicion list?
expert_answers: The first thing the field team wants is the photo (or video) attached to the report — ideally a clear, close, in-focus image of the insect. That single piece of evidence is what distinguishes a genuine Vespa mandarinia from the many look-alikes (other hornets, wasps, even large flies), and it is the strongest predictor of whether a report is a true positive. If no usable image exists, the next most valuable item is a precise location and the date/time of the sighting, since those determine whether a follow-up visit is even feasible within the queen's ~30 km dispersal range and the current season.

The person most likely to have a physical specimen is someone who was already actively engaged with the insect before reporting — typically a beekeeper, a gardener/farmer, or a hobbyist who keeps or studies insects. These people tend to be near hives or gardens where hornets are seen, often have the habit of catching or trapping insects, and know that a specimen is worth preserving rather than swatting. A beekeeper in particular has strong incentive (protecting hives) and the practical means to net a hornet and put it in a jar or freezer.

By contrast, an ordinary homeowner who just saw something alarming on the porch is far more likely to have killed it messily or let it go, and rarely thinks to keep the body. So among no-photo callers, the beekeeper/agricultural or insect-interested reporter is the best bet for a specimen that can be sent to the lab.

Realistically, a state agriculture department in an active scare can field-verify on the order of **a few dozen reports per month** — roughly 20–60 — with a small dedicated team (a handful of entomologists/inspectors, often 2–5 people splitting time with other duties). That translates to a few site visits per working day at most, since each follow-up (travel, inspection, specimen handling, paperwork) consumes hours.

This is an empirical judgment, not a fixed figure. Capacity scales with staffing and season: it may reach ~100/month if the state stands up a surge team at the peak of a scare, and drop to well under 20/month in the off-season. The key point is that confirmed-sighting capacity is far smaller than the ~4,400 reports in the dataset, so triage is unavoidable.

The single most trust-building element is **corroboration by an independent, knowledgeable observer** — a second report of the same insect at the same place and time, or a report from someone who knows insects (beekeeper, entomologist, extension agent) who describes the hornet's distinctive features accurately (large size, orange-and-black head, the "giant" scale) rather than just "a big scary hornet."

What most makes me doubt a report is a **vague or generic description combined with a location/time that doesn't fit** — e.g., "huge hornet on my porch" with no distinguishing detail, reported in winter or far outside the known detection area, or a story that matches a common look-alike (yellowjacket, bald-faced hornet, cicada killer) more than Vespa mandarinia. Reports that arrive in clusters after media coverage, with no physical evidence, are especially suspect.

For a report near a known active area, the team should move within **roughly 1–3 days**, and ideally the same day if the sighting is fresh.

The reason is biological, not bureaucratic: a worker hornet is mobile and a nest can be located and destroyed only while the trail is warm. A live sighting's value decays fast — within about a week the insect has moved on or died, and the location clue is stale. In the active season (late summer/fall, when nests are large and workers forage widely), a fresh confirmed-area report is worth a near-immediate visit; after ~1 week it is usually only worth chasing if a specimen or nest was actually found.

This is an empirical judgment. The practical cutoff is: **same-day to 3 days for a fresh sighting; beyond ~1 week, deprioritize** unless new corroborating reports cluster at the same spot.

Officials declare eradication only after **several consecutive years with zero confirmed positives** — typically **3 years** (some programs use 2, others up to 5) — with no live hornet, nest, or confirmed specimen found anywhere in the state despite continued surveillance.

The reason for the multi-year window is the hornet's life cycle: overwintering queens can persist undetected in soil, and a small residual population can stay cryptic for a season or two. So a single quiet year proves nothing; you need enough consecutive negative years to make a surviving breeding population statistically implausible.

Crucially, "gone" is judged against **active surveillance**, not passive absence of reports. Officials keep looking — trapping, sentinel hives, and public reporting — throughout that period, and the clock only counts years in which that surveillance was actually maintained. If surveillance lapses, the negative years don't count.

This is an empirical judgment; the exact number of years is a policy choice balancing confidence against cost.

Handle it like the others — triage it, don't rush it.

A sighting far from any known nest is, on priors, far more likely to be a mistaken ID than a genuine new incursion, so it does not earn the same-day urgency that a report near a known active area does. The exception is if it comes with strong corroboration — a clear photo, a physical specimen, or a knowledgeable observer (beekeeper, entomologist) describing the hornet accurately. In that case it jumps the queue, because a true positive far from known nests is exactly the signal that the pest has spread and is the most important thing to catch early.

Absent that corroboration, it goes into the normal prioritization: photo quality, reporter credibility, season, and clustering with other reports. Distance from a known nest by itself lowers priority, not raises it.

Expect a **large, short-lived spike** — typically **several-fold to an order of magnitude** above baseline call volume in the days right after a nest is announced, then decaying over roughly **1–3 weeks** back toward baseline (with a smaller echo if follow-up coverage runs).

Which calls surge most: **low-quality, no-evidence reports from the general public** — vague "big scary hornet" sightings, often with no photo, no specimen, and generic descriptions. These are the mistaken-ID calls driven by media attention and anxiety, and they cluster geographically near the news coverage rather than near actual detections. Reports from knowledgeable observers (beekeepers, entomologists) rise much less, since those people were already reporting.

Practical consequence: the spike inflates volume without proportionally inflating true positives, so the **positive rate per report drops sharply** during the surge. This is an empirical judgment; the exact multiplier depends on how prominent the coverage is.

Treat it as the **same infestation continuing**, not a new outbreak — unless there is positive evidence of a separate introduction.

The reason is the life cycle: the hornets overwinter as mated queens in soil, and the workers and old nest die off in the cold. So the first hornets seen in spring are almost always new queens emerging from overwintering sites near last year's activity, founding colonies in the same general area. A gap of a few months with no sightings is expected dormancy, not eradication.

The practical consequence for your model: the winter gap should **not** reset the clock or the spatial prior. Spring detections near last season's confirmed area are the same population and should be treated as high-priority continuity; only a spring sighting far outside the known range, with corroboration, would suggest a genuinely new incursion.

This is an empirical judgment based on the species' biology.

During peak season, check new reports **daily** — the 1–3 day freshness window means a report held for a weekly batch is often already stale by the time you act on it. So the intake/triage step runs daily, even if the field visits themselves are scheduled in small batches (a few per day, grouped by geography to save travel).

Refresh the suspicion list **daily to every few days** during peak season, because that is the cadence at which new reports, new confirmations, and clustering signals actually change the ranking. In the off-season, weekly (or slower) is fine.

The practical split: **daily triage and re-ranking; batched field deployment.** The list should be re-scored whenever a new confirmed positive or a cluster of corroborated reports arrives, since those events shift priorities more than routine volume does. This is an empirical judgment based on the freshness decay and staffing constraints discussed earlier.
